topic: Best-of-N Coding Agents With LLM-as-a-Verifier in Oh My Pi

key_points: The subject of this guide: an MIT-licensed Oh My Pi plugin (70 stars, 53 commits, last push 2026-09-02) that runs N headless OMP candidate sessions in isolated copy-on-write workspaces and ranks full trajectories.
Command surface is deliberately small: `/best-of --n 5 --apply Fix the failing authentication test` in-session, or `omp-best-of --n 3 --apply -- "..."` standalone writing a JSON summary to stdout.

Requirements: Oh My Pi 17+, Bun 1.3+, Git, `uv` (logprob backend only, runs pinned llm-verifier==0.2.0 sidecar), plus a verifier route in omp; a clean working tree is enforced before any candidate starts.

Two backends with the same three criteria (Requirements / Correctness / Verification): default `logprob` (upstream continuous-score pivot tournament) and `sampled` (2 sandboxed candidate audits + seeded all-pairs judge on a subscription model such as openai-codex/gpt-5.6-luna).

Default `--n` is 3, default verifier is deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash, default is selection-only (`--apply` off); a candidate that exits non-zero or whose patch cannot be captured is excluded before ranking.

Maintainers explicitly disclaim the upstream paper's benchmarks: 'the sampled backend is a separate conventional pairwise judge, not the paper's continuous-score method', and 'this plugin has not established equivalent reliability'.
A competing implementation of the same paper for opencode/Claude Code/Grok: `/ultra` runs the task N times in isolated git worktrees and uses the SAME model as verifier — no cross-model dependency.

Key architectural insight others miss: selection can never beat oracle@N, so v2 adds verifier-guided repair on the winner and keeps it only if it verifies better — 91.7% on a 24-task SWE-bench Lite slice vs its own 87.5% oracle@5 ceiling.

Reports 90.4% on the Terminal-Bench 2.1 coding subset (77 tasks) with a small non-vision flash model at best-of-5, vs 89.5%/89.1%/88.4% pass@1 for GPT-5.6 Sol / Claude Opus 5 / Grok 4.6 — framed as reaching the tier at a fraction of cost, not a like-for-like beat.
Honest negative result worth citing: 'planning-first best-of-N does nothing for execution tasks' — drafting N plans, picking one, executing once changed 0 of 5 outcomes at 3-10x cost.

Named failure mode: the verifier saturates on convincing-but-wrong self-reports (a failing run claiming '4102 entries, zero mismatches' when the answer was 698), so pure code diffs are the clean signal and terminal self-reports are not.
The upstream framework everything here depends on (Kwok et al., arXiv 2607.05391; 3.2k stars, MIT) — pip install llm-verifier, with `select()`, `compare()` and token accounting.

Core mechanism vs an LLM judge: fine-grained scoring granularity, expectation over the full logprob distribution of score tokens (not argmax), then scaling repeated evaluation and criteria decomposition.

Publishes a self-verification table on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with DeepSeek V4 Flash for both generation and verification: Best-of-3 79.4% random -> 86.5% verifier-selected, oracle 92.1%; Best-of-5 78.7% -> 88.0%, oracle 96.6%.
Cross-benchmark test-time scaling: Terminal-Bench V2 86.5% (GPT-5.5 best-of-5, Capy, 83.1% -> 86.5%), SWE-Bench Verified 78.2% (best-of-3), MedAgentBench 73.3% (best-of-5).
0.2.0 adds prefix-cache optimization (~3.4x fewer uncached input tokens on trajectory-heavy benchmarks) — the fix for the cost problem that dominates long-trajectory verification.
Needs a backend that returns token logprobs: DeepSeek, vLLM/SGLang, OpenAI-compatible servers; a Claude Code plugin (TurboAgent) is published alongside.
Frames best-of-N as an architecture decision, not benchmark seasoning: vertical scaling (bigger model) vs horizontal scaling (more samples from a cheap model).
Cites the Large Language Monkeys result: a mid-tier open model solved 15.9% of SWE-bench Lite with one attempt and 56% with 250 attempts — beating the single-attempt SOTA of 43% at the time.
Where best-of-N pays: the middle band, where single-shot success is neither ~0 nor ~1 — exactly the regime the maintainers' saturated pools failed to reach.

Selector engineering checklist: randomize candidate order and evaluate both orders (debias), strip length cues, use a judge from a different model family, prefer pairwise tournaments (N-1 comparisons), decompose the verdict into narrow aspect verifiers, and calibrate judge-vs-human agreement against a labeled gold set.
Latency is max-of-N plus the judge pass, not sum-of-N, and shared prompt prefixes are usually billed once — so the marginal cost of extra attempts is lower than it looks.

The most practically useful math for an N-selection: with per-attempt success p, coverage is 1-(1-p)^k — p=50% gives 87.5% at N=3 and 96.9% at N=5; p=25% gives 57.8% at N=3; returns diminish sharply past N=10.
Distinguishes best-of-N from retry explicitly: every candidate runs to completion even if the first succeeds — parallel exploration, not failure recovery.
Multi-signal scoring recipe a verifier could adopt: test pass rate, diff size, linter, type checker, and regression tests, weighted (tests 0.35, regression 0.35).

Cost reality check: on SWE-bench Verified a top agent costs roughly $0.35-$0.75 per instance per attempt, so best-of-5 is $1.75-$3.75 and best-of-10 is $3.50-$7.50 — vs a loaded developer hour at ~$150.
Cost-control patterns worth copying: adaptive N by estimated difficulty, early termination once a candidate passes all tests, and best-of-N with a top-K refinement phase.

Production counterpoint to benchmark verifiers: critics trained only on benchmark traces translate poorly, scoring AUC ~0.45-0.48 (worse than random) on real outcomes, vs 0.69 when trained with code-survival supervision.
Their trajectory critic is small and fast (sub-second to ~1s) enough to run inside an interactive session, enabling both best-of-N selection and early stopping.

Measured inference-time payoff on the mixed-outcome subset of SWE-bench Verified: Best@8 73.8% with the critic vs 57.9% random@8; early stopping is +17.7 over random while averaging only 1.35 attempts.
Frames verification as a layered stack — trajectory-level critic first, more layers later — rather than a single pass/fail judge.

Academic statement of the real bottleneck: long-horizon coding agents 'violate the premise' that outputs can be directly compared, ranked or refined — the challenge is representing prior experience, not generating more attempts.

Converts each rollout into a structured summary preserving hypotheses, progress and failure modes, then scales it two ways: Recursive Tournament Voting (parallel) and Parallel-Distill-Refine (sequential).
Reported gains: Claude-4.5-Opus 70.9% -> 77.6% on SWE-Bench Verified (mini-SWE-agent) and 46.9% -> 59.1% on Terminal-Bench v2.0 (Terminus 1).
Directly relevant to trajectory-length limits: the compression step is what makes ranking long agent rollouts tractable at all.

stats.fact: LLM-as-a-Verifier reports SOTA on Terminal-Bench V2 86.5%, SWE-Bench Verified 78.2%, RoboRewardBench 87.4% and MedAgentBench 73.3%.

Upstream self-verification on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with DeepSeek V4 Flash for generation and verification: best-of-3 79.4% random -> 86.5% verifier-selected (oracle 92.1%); best-of-5 78.7% -> 88.0% (oracle 96.6%).

omp-best-of's own measured, still-standing results: logprob 1 evaluation 5/10 (50.0%) selections correct against a 62.5% random pass@1 baseline; sampled Luna 1 round 13/15 (86.7%) against a 32.0% random baseline over five reused discriminating pools (ancestor commit 06eefab).
The plugin's earlier six-pool sampled headlines of 83.3% and 72.2% are withdrawn: two pools (content-type, http-range) had defective oracles and no candidate passes the corrected oracles.

On saturated pools the verifier's score spread collapsed to 0.000-0.006 (nearly every comparison a tie, so the reported winner was a tie-break) and re-ranking one pool three times with identical settings and seed picked #2, #4, #2.

On the single discriminating pool with real separation (0.061), the verifier ranked a failing candidate first at both 1 and 3 evaluations per criterion; repeated evaluation tripled cost without improving selection.

Verification was 25-51% of live-run cost in the plugin's early runs, because the verifier reads long trajectories and its output/reasoning tokens dominate the bill (run C retry-transient: 147,533 of 153,547 output tokens were reasoning).

Practical per-task budget on small fixtures: ~$0.0084-$0.0119 per candidate run, i.e. roughly $0.04-$0.05 for a 4-candidate pool and $0.05-$0.08 including verification; one 4-candidate task took 95s-693s end to end.
Sampled ranking cost model: 2N + E*N(N-1)/2 verifier invocations for N candidates and E evaluations — 14 invocations for four candidates at one evaluation, 44 for eight.
Verifier-guided repair beats the selection ceiling: on a 24-task SWE-bench Lite slice agent-ultramode reaches 91.7% against its own 87.5% oracle@5, by rescuing two tasks no attempt solved.
Same-model best-of-5 with a verifier reached 90.4% on the Terminal-Bench 2.1 coding subset (77 tasks) with a small non-vision flash model; blended 78.7% base -> 87.6%, a +8.9 point lift.
Planning-first best-of-N is a measured dead end: drafting N plans, selecting one, then executing once changed 0 of 5 outcomes on Terminal-Bench at 3-10x the cost.
Coverage math: 1-(1-p)^k. At p=50%, N=3 gives 87.5% and N=5 gives 96.9%; at p=25%, N=3 gives 57.8%; at p=10%, N=20 only reaches 87.8%.
Large Language Monkeys: a mid-tier open model went from 15.9% on SWE-bench Lite with one attempt to 56% with 250 attempts, above the 43% single-attempt SOTA of the time.
Cost baseline for coding agents: roughly $0.35-$0.75 per SWE-bench Verified instance per attempt, so best-of-5 is $1.75-$3.75 and best-of-10 $3.50-$7.50.

Critics trained only on benchmark traces score AUC ~0.45-0.48 (worse than random) on production outcomes; training on code survival lifts it to 0.69. Critic-guided Best@8 hit 73.8% vs 57.9% random@8 on mixed-outcome SWE-bench Verified.
Representation-based test-time scaling for agentic coding: Claude-4.5-Opus improved 70.9% -> 77.6% on SWE-Bench Verified and 46.9% -> 59.1% on Terminal-Bench v2.0.
stats.source: arXiv 2604.16529, 'Scaling Test-Time Compute for Agentic Coding'

stats.fact: Ecosystem size check: Oh My Pi (can1357/oh-my-pi) has ~33.9k stars and pushes daily; the upstream verifier repo has ~3.2k stars; omp-best-of itself has 70 stars and 53 commits.

angles: Selection, not generation, is the bottleneck: coverage climbs log-linearly with samples, but picking the winner is a separate, harder problem — the guide's thesis and the reason the paper exists.

The oracle@N ceiling is the honest framing: best-of-N can never beat the best attempt it was handed, which is why repair passes past that ceiling (91.7% vs 87.5%) matter more than another point of selection accuracy.

Two backends, two contracts: logprob needs an endpoint that honors constrained prefill and returns score-token distributions (vLLM/SGLang are eligible), sampled works on subscription routes with no API credits — pick by what your credentials can prove, and never present sampled as the paper's method.

Read the maintainers' own numbers before believing the headline: 50% logprob selections on two reused tasks, score spread collapsing to 0.000-0.006 on saturated pools, a discriminating pool ranked wrongly, and two withdrawn 80%+ claims due to oracle defects.

Cost model surprises: verification is 25-51% of live-run cost because the verifier reads long trajectories and reasons over them; three evaluations tripled the bill for zero accuracy gain, which is why the default stays at one.

Latency, not money, is the wall: candidates run concurrently within a task but tasks run sequentially, so wall clock ranged 95s-693s per 4-candidate task — task-level parallelism is the obvious next optimization.

Saturate-or-discriminate: to measure anything you need pools with headroom AND trajectories containing validation evidence; visible tests give the second and destroy the first, so harden the hidden contract instead of deleting the tests.

Verifier blind spots: plausible-looking code plus visible validation can outrank a correct patch that missed an unobserved contract edge case, and self-reported terminal outcomes are actively dangerous to trust.

Isolation is not a sandbox: candidate workspaces prevent patch collisions only — candidates run headless in yolo approval mode with host filesystem and network access, so treat them like any unsandboxed subprocess.

Do the easy wins first: adaptive N by difficulty, early exit as soon as a candidate passes your tests (1.35 attempts average in OpenHands' early-stopping measurement), and pairwise tournaments instead of absolute 1-10 scores.
